checks.claim: Ioannidis, a physician(-scientist), published 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' in PLoS Medicine in 2005

Stem paraphrase: the more ideas tested and the less carefully chosen, the less likely findings are true (Corollary 3: 'The greater the number and the lesser the selection of tested relationships in a scientific field, the less likely the research findings are to be true')

Key 'About five in every six': 99 false x 1/20 = about 5 false passes beside 1 true pass, so 5 of 6 passes false; fits his model PPV = (1-beta)R/(R - betaR + alpha) with R = 1/99, power 1, alpha 0.05, PPV = 0.17
Wrong choices 'one in six', 'one in twenty', 'one in two' are each wrong for the stated numbers (one in six is the true share; one in twenty is the alpha slip; one in two has no basis)

Context: his remedies were larger studies, upfront registration and the totality of the evidence ('Better powered evidence, e.g., large studies or low-bias meta-analyses, may help'; 'upfront registration of studies'; 'What matters is the totality of the evidence')
Context: even a fair test passes more flukes than truths when few ideas tested are true (paper blames chance and bias, not fraud)

Context: Jager and Leek (Biostatistics 2014) said the model rested on assumptions ('justifiable but arbitrary assumptions rather than empirical data') and estimated the false share at about 14 percent
checks.note: Their 14% (s.d. 1%) is a science-wise false discovery rate estimated from p-values in abstracts of five top medical journals, 2000-2010 (Biostatistics 15(1):1-12). 'in biomedical studies' follows Wikipedia; 'in top medical journals' would be more exact. Not an error.

checks.claim: Button, Ioannidis, Mokrysz, Nosek, Flint, Robinson, Munafo, 'Power failure', Nature Reviews Neuroscience 14:365-376, 2013; Button first author, Munafo senior author
Median statistical power of a neuroscience study about 21 percent (49 meta-analyses of 2011, about 730 studies)
checks.note: 'a typical study' fairly renders the median. Nord et al. 2017 showed power is heterogeneous; the card need not say so.

checks.claim: Key: low power lowers the share of passes that are real (abstract: 'low power also reduces the likelihood that a statistically significant result reflects a true effect')
Wrong choices: 'leaves it alone', 'raises it', 'lowers it because small studies are faked' are each wrong (the argument turns on chance, not fraud)
Context: Ioannidis, one of the team, argued in 2005 that smaller studies and smaller effects make findings less likely true (Corollaries 1 and 2); remedy better-powered evidence such as large studies
Context paraphrase of Button's key point (low power from small samples, small effects or both lowers the likelihood that a significant result reflects a true effect); not in quotation marks
Brian Nosek, University of Virginia, led about 270 researchers (Open Science Collaboration)
checks.note: Grokipedia 'over 270'; Science News '270'.

checks.claim: 100 studies published in 2008 in three journals (Psychological Science, JPSP, JEP: LMC); original authors consulted
97 of the originals significant; 35 of 97 significant again (36 percent); key 'About a third of them'
checks.note: Science News: 'Only 35 of 97 reports of statistically significant results' replicated; abstract gives 36%.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'two thirds', 'nearly all', 'one in ten' are wrong
Context: replication effects on average about half the original size (r = 0.197 against 0.403)
Context: the team could not say whether failures meant false originals, missed real effects, or unnoticed differences
Reported in 2015 (Science 349, 28 August 2015)
Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn, 'False-Positive Psychology', Psychological Science 2011
20 University of Pennsylvania undergraduates heard 'When I'm Sixty-Four' or another tune ('Kalimba'), then gave birth dates
checks.note: 20 is the count in the reported version; the disclosed version had 34 students across three songs, the 20 being those in the two reported conditions. The stem is true.

checks.claim: Reported result: Beatles listeners 'nearly a year-and-a-half younger' (adjusted 20.1 against 21.5), significant
Key: they set out to show that common, flexible data handling can make a false result look real
Wrong choices (results made up by authors; students misreport birth dates; a song makes listeners feel younger) are wrong; the data were real and the point was flexibility, not fraud
Context: they added students until the result crossed the line (analysed after every session of about 10), chose afterwards what to adjust for (father's age), and left out some of the groups tested
checks.note: They dropped ONE condition (the Wiggles' 'Hot Potato'). 'left out one of the groups they had tested' would be exact; 'some of the groups' is a loose plural, not a false claim.

checks.claim: Context: simulations of four such choices combined gave a false-positive rate of about 61 percent (60.7%) against the nominal 5 percent
checks.note: 60.7% per secondary sources and Grokipedia; Penn Gazette and APS give 61 percent.

checks.claim: Andrew Gelman (statistician, Columbia) and Eric Loken, 'The garden of forking paths' (14 November 2013)
Scenario: one honest test whose choice depended on the data (subgroup where the effect looks strongest)
checks.note: The paper's case is 'a single test based on the data, in an environment where a different test would have been performed given different data'; the 'older half' detail is the writer's illustration, not their example (the judge's rewording, 'argued in 2013 that ... Suppose a researcher ...', removes the implication).

checks.claim: Key: had the scores fallen otherwise he would have run another test (the p-value is a statement about what would have been done had the data been different)
Wrong choices (sample too small; 1-in-20 line too loose for one test; broke the rules by leaving out half) are not their argument
Context: can happen even when the hypothesis was set out ahead of time, with no fishing; they called it the garden of forking paths
Context: its chance of passing by luck was 'far above 1 in 20'
checks.note: Gelman and Loken give no figure. For the stem's one fork (older half, younger half or all), the inflation is modest: Simmons et al.'s single comparable choice (report one of three conditions) gave about 12.6%, not 'far above'. Fix: 'its chance of passing by luck was above 1 in 20, by more the more paths the data could have sent him down'.

checks.claim: Context: cure is to set the analysis down before seeing the data, or test the new idea again on fresh data
checks.note: Gelman and Loken recommend preregistered replication; consistent.

checks.claim: Robert Rosenthal named the 'file drawer problem' in 1979 (Psychological Bulletin 86(3))
Franco, Malhotra and Simonovits followed 221 experiments (of 249) run through TESS, an NSF-funded program, 2002-2012
Most null-result studies never published (about 20 percent published)

Key: their own authors never wrote them up ('nearly 65 percent of the studies with null findings were not only not published, but never even written up'; 'authors do not write up and submit null findings')
Wrong choices (editors, reviewers, funders) are not the main cause found
Context: reasons were expected rejection or lost interest; strong results 40 percentage points more likely to be published than null
Context: they called for studies to be registered before they are run
checks.note: BITSS summary: 'requirements to pre-register studies' and two-stage review.

checks.claim: Daryl Bem, Cornell, nine experiments, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2011, apparently showing precognition
Ritchie, Wiseman and French repeated one experiment (retroactive facilitation of recall) in three labs, 50 students each, no effect
Key: JPSP rejected it under a policy against publishing replications
Quote: 'on the basis that the journal has a policy of not publishing replications' (Chris French)
checks.note: Matches word for word: 'Our submission was rejected without being sent for peer review on the basis that the journal has a policy of not publishing replications'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (not planned ahead; too few students; altered method) are false: pre-registered, power analysis called for 41 and they ran 50 per lab, Bem's own program and word list
checks.note: Five words of the 48 were swapped for UK-familiar ones; not an altered method in any sense the journal cited.

checks.claim: Context: PLoS ONE printed it in 2012 (14 March)
Context: later in 2012 JPSP printed seven failed repeats by Jeff Galak and colleagues
checks.note: Galak, LeBoeuf, Nelson, Simmons, JPSP 103(6):933-948, December 2012; seven experiments, 3,289 participants.

checks.claim: Stapel, Dutch social psychologist, fabricated data he said came from contacts at schools
Key: three young researchers in his own department first reported him, 2011
checks.note: Nature/SciAm: 'three young researchers under Stapel's supervision'; they went to Marcel Zeelenberg, head of the Department of Social Psychology.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (a peer reviewer, a failed replication, a journal editor) did not first report him
Context: late August 2011, to department head Marcel Zeelenberg; asked for his schools, Stapel said they did not exist
checks.note: Wikipedia: when the rector asked for the contacts, 'Stapel said the schools did not actually exist'.

checks.claim: Context: telltale data: large effects, rare missing data and outliers, hypotheses rarely refuted
Quote: Pim Levelt, 'the scientific checks and balances process has failed at several levels'
checks.note: Full: 'We see that the scientific checks and balances process has failed at several levels.' The quoted part matches word for word.

checks.claim: Context: final report of 2012 (28 November) counted 55 fraudulent publications
Schon, Bell Labs physicist; in 2001 an author on about one new paper every eight days; many in Nature and Science
Lydia Sohn, then at Princeton, saw in 2002 that two experiments at very different temperatures had identical noise
checks.note: Hsu and Loo noticed duplicated data first (19 April 2002, while preparing a patent). The stem does not call Sohn the first, so it stands.

checks.claim: Key: 'The two graphs came from one measurement, not two'
checks.note: Matching noise shows one data set was used twice; it does not show that set was ever measured, and the committee found some curves were 'produced using mathematical functions'. Fix: 'The two graphs came from one set of data, not two' (as the judge also proposed).

checks.claim: Wrong choices (same machine, same day, devices behaved alike) are wrong: random noise does not repeat
Context: Schon told Nature he had sent the same graph twice by mistake ('accidentally submitted the same graph twice')
Context: Paul McEuen of Cornell found the same noise in a third experiment
Context: committee report September 2002 (25 September): whole data sets reused, some curves from mathematical functions; no lab notebooks; raw data erased; no other lab reproduced his results
Chris Chambers launched registered reports at Cortex in 2013
checks.note: Cortex began offering the format in May 2013.

checks.claim: Reviewers judge question and plan before data; journal commits to publish 'regardless of the outcome, provided the approved protocol is followed'
Scheel, Schijen and Lakens 2021: 96% positive in standard reports against 44% in registered reports (first hypothesis); key 'Nearly all ordinary papers, but under half of registered reports'
Wrong choices (both high; reversed; both about half) are wrong
Context: the gap stayed large without direct replications (96 against 50)
checks.note: 'remained nearly as large when direct replications were excluded'.

checks.claim: Context: authors wrote the gap suggests psychologists underreport negative results; study did not directly test whether registered reports reduce bias
checks.note: Paraphrase, not in quotation marks; faithful.

unit_notes: All ten checked on the web. Two uncertain, none wrong. Q5 (770a4885d5): the card's 'far above 1 in 20' overstates the inflation from the stem's single fork; say 'above 1 in 20'. Q9 (199196b084): the key 'one measurement' should be 'one set of data', since some of Schon's curves were never measured. Quotations checked word for word: French (ScienceDaily 2012) and Levelt (Nature/SciAm 2011) match. Ioannidis's model fits the Q1 worked example (PPV = 0.17). OSC: 35 of 97 significant again = 36%. Hsu and Loo noticed the duplication before Sohn; no stem says Sohn was first.
